passages.title: Different Customs Around the World
passages.body: When you visit a foreign country, it is important to learn about its customs. In some countries, people are supposed to shake hands when they meet. In Japan, people are supposed to bow instead. In some places, friends greet each other with a kiss on the cheek. Time also matters. In Switzerland, you are supposed to be on time. It is impolite to keep others waiting. But in some warm countries, people are more relaxed about time. Knowing these customs helps us make a good first impression. After all, good manners are important everywhere, even if they are different from place to place.

passages.title: Maria's First Dinner
passages.body: Maria is an exchange student in the US. Last night, she had dinner at an American friend's house. Maria made a few mistakes because she did not know the customs. First, she arrived late. In the US, you are supposed to arrive on time. Then, she ate the food before everyone else started. You are supposed to wait until everyone is ready. She also greeted her friend's mother in the wrong way. But her friend's family was very kind. They were not mad at her. They helped her learn. By the end of the evening, Maria felt much more relaxed. She learned that it is important to learn local customs.

passages.title: Is It OK to Be Late?
passages.body: People in different countries have different ideas about time. Teresa is from Colombia. She says it is OK to be a little late when meeting friends. "We value people more than time," she says. If a friend is late, she does not get mad. Marc is from Switzerland. For him, being on time is very important. "We are the capital of clocks and watches," he says. If someone invites you to dinner at seven, you are supposed to arrive at seven. Both ideas are fine in their own countries. The most important thing is to learn the local custom, so that you do not make others uneasy.

passages.title: Table Manners Around the World
passages.body: Table manners are different around the world. In some countries, you are supposed to use chopsticks. In others, you use a knife and fork. In India, people often eat with their right hand, but you are not supposed to use your left hand. In China, it is impolite to stick your chopsticks into your food. In some Western countries, you are not supposed to put your elbows on the table. In Japan, it is polite to make noise when you eat noodles. So when you travel, remember: what is polite in one country may be rude in another. The best advice is to watch what others do.

passages.title: Yu Mei's Letter from France
passages.body: Dear Laura, How are you? I am an exchange student in France now, and I am learning a lot. At first, I made many mistakes with the customs. For example, in France, you are not supposed to put your bread on your plate. You are supposed to put it on the table! Also, when you have dinner, you are expected to keep both hands on the table. At home, I was taught the opposite. The biggest challenge is the food. There is so much of it! But my host family is very kind. They go out of their way to make me feel at home. Gradually, I am getting used to life here. Yours, Yu Mei

passages.title: Welcome Guide for Exchange Students
passages.body: WELCOME TO OUR SCHOOL! This guide will help you learn our customs. GREETINGS: When you meet a teacher, you are supposed to say "Good morning." It is polite to be friendly. ON TIME: You are expected to arrive at class on time. It is impolite to be late. IN CLASS: You are not supposed to use your phone. Please turn it off. AT LUNCH: You are supposed to wait in line. Do not push others. WITH FRIENDS: It is polite to share and help each other. If you are not sure what to do, just ask. We hope you will feel at home here. Enjoy your time with us!
